newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU parliament to seek shake-up in EU farm sector.
newsitem.headline: EU parliament to seek shake-up in EU farm sector.

text.p: Members of the European Parliament, using new investigative powers to try to ease consumer fears over mad cow disease, are expected to demand a major shake-up of the European Commission's veterinary services to end a conflict of interest.

A special committee of inquiry into the epidemic, which has ravaged British herds and scared shoppers across the continent, has, over the past three months, questioned whether the Commission and member states have put profit before public health.
On Tuesday, the 19-member cross-party committee will interrogate European Union Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler and Britain's Chief Veterinary Officer Keith Meldrum.
Fischler will be grilled about a confidential report ordered last year which is believed to call for a sweeping restructuring of the veterinary services.
"Fischler will be asked to explain the report," Reimer Boge, German Christian Democrat chairman of the committee, told Reuters on Monday. "Things are unclear. Changes are needed."
The questioning will be in private because the document is still secret, added Boge, whose committee is the first to exploit new powers granted under the EU's 1992 Maastricht Treaty.

But the committee is expected, either in a statement later this week or in its final report due in January, to urge that the Commission's veterinary services be hived off from the Commission's directorate general for agriculture.

Animal health would be combined with public health, which is currently part of the employment and social affairs directorate, and then put under the control of the fledgling consumer affairs department.
The powerful agriculture directorate, which manages 50 percent of the total EU budget, is seen as defending the interests of beef farmers.

Former Farm Commissioner Ray MacSharry, who was in charge of EU farm policy when mad cow disease, or Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) peaked in 1992, has strongly denied that protection of human health was put into second place.
"Managing the beef market was never given priority over public health," he told the inquiry last week.

Fischler will also be grilled on why in June he approved a conditional lifting of a ban on exports of British gelatine -- a beef by-product used in food, drugs and cosmetics -- despite a warning from the chemical industry urging more research.
Critics say the move was intended to help pave the way for a compromise with Britain at the Florence EU summit on a phased lifting of the ban subject to fulfilment of strict conditions.

Boge said Meldrum will be closely questioned about the British government's failure to enforce properly a ban on the use of meat and bone meal -- widely believed to be a cause of BSE -- in animal feed, as well as why it blocked EU inspections.
Meldrum is alleged to have told EU inspectors that BSE "was a political not a technical matter" and that they had no right to pry.
But when the Euro MPs sought a political account from British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg, they were twice fobbed off and had to make do with a senior ministry official.
EU commissioners and senior officials have pleaded lack of funds and staff to carry out adequate BSE inspections and argued that it was up to member states to ensure that measures were enforced.
